extracted.intended_audience: registrants (public companies), securities lawyers, compliance officers, investors, and other stakeholders interested in SEC climate-related disclosure rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for what climate-related information public companies must disclose in SEC filings, how that information should be prepared, where it should be placed, and related assurance/controls and alignment with other reporting frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greenwashing (concept/outside definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission did not define 'greenwashing' in the Proposing Release and is not defining it now. As a general matter, others have defined greenwashing to mean the set of activities conducted by firms or funds to falsely convey to investors that their investment products or practices are aligned with environmental or other ESG principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While SEC declines to adopt a formal definition here, regulators and commenters treat greenwashing as misrepresentations or false impressions about alignment with environmental/ESG principles; see IOSCO Supervisory Practices to Address Greenwashing (Dec. 2023).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized, comparable, timely, reliable disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Many commenters argued that consistent, standardized disclosures addressing climate-related risks and opportunities help investors make decisions and improve informational and allocative efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters (e.g., CalSTRS, PwC, Bank of America) stated that mandatory disclosure in annual filings would enhance comparability and ensure timeliness, quality, and reliability of climate information so it is commensurate with financial data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of climate-related disclosures in SEC filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended placement of climate-related disclosure either in a separate section of the filing, in MD&A (Management's Discussion & Analysis) or the Operating and Financial Review (OFR), or in other existing sections of the annual report or registration statement, as applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some supporters favored a separate section plus inclusion elsewhere; others recommended placing financial-disclosure-level climate information in MD&A or notes to financial statements to ensure comparability and scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion in annual and (where appropriate) quarterly reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters stated the disclosures mandated by the SEC should be filed in annual reports, as well as quarterly reports where appropriate, so they are subject to disclosure controls, CEO/CFO certification, and audit requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing in periodic reports subjects climate information to the same processes and scrutiny as other required disclosure, increasing investor confidence and comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurance requirements (example: California SB-253)
rubrics_metrics.description: California SB-253 requires disclosure of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions to be subject to assurance: limited assurance beginning in 2026 and reasonable assurance beginning in 2030 (statute currently subject to litigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This state-law example indicates a trajectory toward increasing levels of assurance over time for GHG emissions; commenters referenced such models when discussing the SEC's approach to assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of GHG Protocol-aligned emissions reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters (e.g., PIMCO, Vanguard, Allyson Tucker/Washington State Investment Board) supported inclusion of a greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reporting requirement in line with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GHG Protocol alignment was recommended to help investors understand emissions as they relate to company financial performance and earnings quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference from sustainability/corporate responsibility reports (caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters (e.g., PwC) expressed concern about permitting registrants to incorporate by reference from sustainability reports or corporate responsibility reports because such reports 'may be prepared using a basis of presentation designed for a stakeholder group with different information needs than investors and other providers of capital.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because external sustainability reports may target different audiences, reliance on incorporation by reference could undermine comparability, timeliness, and investor-focused presentation of climate-related information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition/use of ISSB/IFRS S1 and S2 and TCFD frameworks (international standards alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: IFRS S1 sets out general requirements for disclosure of sustainability-related financial information; IFRS S2 sets out requirements for climate-related disclosures. TCFD recommendations have been incorporated into the ISSB standards. Commenters suggested using ISSB as an alternative reporting regime, but the Commission declined to recognize ISSB as an alternative reporting regime at this time because jurisdictions have not yet integrated ISSB standards into their rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rulemaking considers international standards (ISSB/IFRS, TCFD) and developments in other jurisdictions (UK SDS, EU CSRD, Australia drafts) for alignment, but does not currently permit ISSB as a substitute reporting regime for SEC requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid boilerplate; require specificity and depth in disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff observed that disclosures in registrants' Forms 10-K frequently contained general, boilerplate discussions that provide limited information as to the registrants' assessment of their climate-related risks or their impact on the companies' business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective disclosure should go beyond generic statements to provide detailed, registrant-specific analysis of climate-related risks, their financial impacts, and how they are managed—improving usefulness and comparability for investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure controls and procedures (Exchange Act Rules 13a-15 and 15d-15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rules 13a-15 and 15d-15, a company's principal executive officer and principal financial officer must make certifications regarding the maintenance and effectiveness of disclosure controls and procedures. 'Disclosure controls and procedures' are defined as those controls and procedures designed to ensure that information required to be disclosed by the company in the reports that it files or submits under the Exchange Act is (1) 'recorded, processed, summarized and reported, within the time periods specified in the Commission's rules and forms,' and (2) 'accumulated and communicated to the company's management . . . as appropriate to allow timely decisions regarding required disclosure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Climate-related information filed with the SEC should be captured by and subject to these disclosure controls and related officer certifications to ensure accuracy and timely reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of disclosure controls — capture information potentially subject to disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A company's disclosure controls and procedures should not be limited to disclosure specifically required, but should also ensure timely collection and evaluation of 'information potentially subject to [required] disclosure,' 'information that is relevant to an assessment of the need to disclose developments and risks that pertain to the [company's] businesses,' and 'information that must be evaluated in the context of the disclosure requirement of Exchange Act Rule 12b-20.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies must proactively monitor and evaluate information that could trigger disclosure obligations, including climate-related developments, to satisfy disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality as a legal and contested standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters asserted the Commission exceeded its statutory authority by issuing rules requiring disclosure of information that is not financially material and is only of general or environmental interest; they argued the proposal 'sidesteps the materiality requirement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The debate highlights that disclosures should ordinarily be tied to material financial impacts for investors; the Commission and commenters dispute the appropriate scope and interpretation of materiality for climate-related information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability/coverage: which issuers are required to comply
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulemaking cites statutory bases (e.g., Securities Act sections, Exchange Act sections 12(b), 12(g), 13(a), 15(d)) identifying which issuers are required to comply with reporting requirements; other issuers that voluntarily register or file certain statements may also be subject to reporting requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining whether a registrant must provide climate-related disclosures depends on its status under relevant securities statutes and rules (e.g., whether it is an Exchange Act reporting company).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of international and regional regulatory developments
rubrics_metrics.description: The release discusses international developments (EU CSRD/ESRS, UK Sustainability Disclosure Standards, Australia draft legislation) and California state laws (e.g., SB-253, SB-261) as context for climate disclosure requirements and assurance expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrants operating across jurisdictions should be aware of differing timelines, assurance levels, and reporting standards internationally and at state level; the SEC considered these developments in shaping its approach to comparability and convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: climate-related disclosures can materially affect company valuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters and referenced research asserted that climate-related impacts or risks can materially affect a company's financial position and operations, and that investors need consistent, comparable disclosure to analyze risks, opportunities, and valuations (e.g., due to IRA incentives or extreme weather causing economic losses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure obligations are justified by potential material financial impacts from climate change and policy developments; companies should disclose information enabling investors to evaluate those impacts.
